content: The intervention targeted women, families, and healthcare providers or facilities in rural Bangladesh. It involved multiple components, including community participation in quality improvement (QI) processes. A stakeholder committee was established to gather community feedback on improving services, with responsibilities such as monitoring cleanliness and assessing client perspectives on service quality. Reports were generated to evaluate the fulfillment of emergency obstetric care needs before and after the intervention. Antenatal care (ANC) usage was also assessed. The study had several methodological limitations. The method of randomization and blinding were not described, and data were primarily self-reported through household surveys, though patient records were used for validation when possible (Bjorkman and Svensson, 2009). In a preand post-program evaluation (Sinha, 2008), the reliability and validity of the survey tools were unclear, and the tools themselves were modified between baseline and follow-up. Selection bias was possible, and no information was provided on potential confounding factors. Another retrospective before-and-after study (Purdin, Khan, and Saucier, 2009) was at high risk of bias due to incomplete or unreliable surveillance data, potential selection bias, and the absence of a control group, making it difficult to attribute observed changes solely to the intervention. Indirectness was noted in studies conducted in lowand middle-income countries, including Kenya, India, Pakistan, and Afghanistan, where the populations studied were rural, poor communities, or Afghan refugee women (Purdin, Khan, and Saucier, 2009). Improvements in ANC practices were reported, with significant differences observed between baseline and endline in women who attended at least one or more than three ANC visits (Sinha, 2008). However, a retrospective study reported increased ANC use following the intervention but did not analyze the changes (Purdin, Khan, and Saucier, 2009). Postpartum care coverage within 72 hours of birth was also evaluated. One study (Ahluwalia, 2010) reported significant increases in deliveries assisted by trained personnel and those occurring at health facilities over a three-year follow-up period. However, the study design lacked a control group, making it challenging to determine whether changes were due to the intervention or external factors. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends community participation in quality improvement processes and program planning to improve maternal and newborn health outcomes. Evidence from four studies, including two cluster randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and one quasi-experimental study, showed moderate quality but serious risks of bias and indirectness. While some studies reported increased facility births, results varied widely, and the lack of control groups in observational studies made it difficult to attribute changes to the interventions. In studies evaluating ANC use, two cluster RCTs and one quasi-experimental study of moderate quality reported mixed results. Some studies showed non-significant increases in ANC use, while others reported decreases. Observational studies consistently reported increased ANC use, but the lack of control groups and potential selection bias limited the reliability of these findings. Overall, the evidence quality was rated as very low due to serious risks of bias, indirectness, and inconsistency across studies. The lack of control groups and methodological weaknesses in many studies made it difficult to draw definitive conclusions about the effectiveness of community participation interventions in improving maternal and newborn health outcomes.
